slide.title: New Head, Same Brain
slide.body: A row of grey backbone blocks with a lock icon, and one bright teal head block at the end labelled healthy / disease 1 / disease 2. Small tag: Computer Vision Essentials · Lesson 7.

scenes.on_screen_text: A new task, with little data
scenes.voiceover: In the last lesson, the general model did not know your categories. Training a new model from zero needs a very large labelled dataset. With transfer learning, around a thousand labelled images and a short Colab session can be enough to teach a model a new task.

slide.title: Transfer Learning: Fine-Tuning on Your Own Images

scenes.voiceover: Tomasz, in Gdańsk, needed his own furniture categories, and the general model could not give them. Today, we fix that kind of problem. We take a model that already sees well, and teach it a new job.

slide.title: General layers, specific head
slide.body: Row of layer blocks: edges → textures → shapes → parts (labelled 'general features') → final head block (labelled 'original labels').

scenes.voiceover: Remember from lesson five that image models learn general features in their early and middle layers. Edges, textures, shapes and parts. Only the last layer, the classification head, is specific to the original labels.

slide.title: Keep the backbone, swap the head
slide.body: Backbone blocks stay the same (grey). Old head is crossed out. New teal head with your classes: healthy · disease 1 · disease 2.

scenes.voiceover: Transfer learning keeps the pre-trained layers, called the backbone, and replaces the head with a new one that has your classes. This works with little data, because the backbone already knows what an edge or a leaf vein looks like. Your data only teaches the head which combination of features means rust, or healthy.

slide.title: Two levels
slide.body: Feature extraction: backbone frozen, train head only, fast, little data. Full fine-tuning: update backbone too, small learning rate, more data and time, risk of overfitting. Start left.

scenes.voiceover: There are two common levels. With feature extraction, you freeze the backbone and train only the new head. It is fast and needs little data. With full fine-tuning, you also update the backbone, with a small learning rate. It can fit your data better, but needs more data and time. Start with feature extraction.

slide.title: Good habits
slide.body: Train · validation · test: keep separate · Test split: check once, at the end · Colab GPU: helpful, not guaranteed

scenes.voiceover: Keep your train, validation and test splits separate, and check the test split only once, at the end. And remember that free Colab GPUs are useful here, but they are not guaranteed, and sessions are limited. So save your work when training ends.

scenes.stock_query: photographer sorting printed photos on table
scenes.voiceover: Think of it like hiring an experienced photographer to sort plant photos. They already understand light, shapes and colours. You only show them a few hundred examples of each disease. A beginner would need years. The photographer needs an afternoon.

scenes.stock_query: close up of green bean plant leaves
scenes.voiceover: Let's try it. Grace Namukasa works for an agricultural advice service in Mbale, Uganda. She wants a model that classifies bean leaf photos as healthy, or as one of two diseases. She uses a public bean leaf photo dataset.

screen_steps: Open Runtime, then Change runtime type
Select a GPU if one is available and save
scenes.voiceover: First, in Colab, she opens the runtime settings and chooses a GPU, if one is available. Training is much faster on a GPU. If none is free today, the same code still runs on the processor, only more slowly.

screen_steps: Scroll through the cell: load_dataset, class names, AutoImageProcessor, AutoModelForImageClassification with num_labels
Highlight the loop that sets requires_grad = False on model.base_model.parameters()
scenes.voiceover: Then she walks through the cell. It loads the dataset and the class names, loads a pre-trained vision model with a new head for three classes, and prepares each image the way the model expects. Here is the key line. A short loop freezes every backbone parameter, so only the new head will learn.

screen_steps: Show the training loss decreasing over the 3 epochs
scenes.voiceover: She runs it. Before training, the new head is untrained, so the test accuracy is close to guessing, about one in three. You'll see something like zero point three four. Then the training starts, and the loss goes down, epoch by epoch.

screen_steps: Run trainer.save_model() and show the saved folder in the file panel
scenes.voiceover: After three epochs, the test accuracy is a clearly higher number. Your numbers will differ, and they are not a benchmark. Finally, she saves the model, because she will measure it properly in the next lesson.

Watch for two common mistakes. Reporting accuracy on the training images only shows that the model remembers them, so report the test split. And unfreezing the whole backbone with a high learning rate on a small dataset can destroy the pre-trained features. When you unfreeze, use a small learning rate.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Reuse the backbone, train a new head. 2. Freeze first; unfreeze later with a small learning rate. 3. Separate splits; report the test split.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, transfer learning reuses a pre-trained backbone and trains a new head for your classes, so it needs much less data and time. Second, start by freezing the backbone and training only the head, and unfreeze later only if you have enough data. Third, keep your splits separate, and report results on the test split.

Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will fine-tune a small pre-trained model on a public dataset of three to five classes, and compare its test accuracy before and after. Save your best model, because you will need it next. It takes about forty minutes. In the next lesson, Measuring Classification Quality. See you there.
